speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Since then, the Israeli Defence Force (IDF) has moved into the Gaza with the aim of eliminating the threat from Hamas in self-defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Over the weekend, I listened to stories played on BBC radio, interviewing family members of the victims of this war and those who have been living in the war zone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The humanitarian situation in Gaza is dire and, since this Motion was filed, has gotten worse.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The civilian population has had to deal with shortages of drinking water, power, food and medicines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Isreali blockade is ostensibly to prevent these being used for military purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, this position has been doubted even by leading Jewish lawyers, including former UK Supreme Court President, Lord Neuberger, who reiterated in an open letter that international law requires minimum destruction to civilian life and infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The United Nations, the International Red Cross and other international organisations wish to provide aid and support to the people in Gaza, but have been facing difficulties doing so because of the blockade, as Israeli forces have cited concerns that these supplies may go into the hands of Hamas and be used for military purposes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is why limb (b) advocates for the urgent delivery of humanitarian aid to the civilian population in Gaza.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Since this Motion was filed, events have moved on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the same resolution, the General Assembly of the UN reiterated that unhindered access should be given to United Nations humanitarian agencies, the International Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a recognition that Israel has a positive duty to permit humanitarian access.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, procedurally, I am not able to amend my own Motion if it changes the scope of the debate, so my colleague, Mr Alex Yam, will propose specific amendments to address both these points in his speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Next, limb (c) condemns those responsible for terrorist acts and also violations of international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The ostensible reason for the attack by Hamas against Israel had to do with unhappiness with the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank as well as the clashes at the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unsuspecting civilians in Israel were therefore targeted to send a political message by Hamas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Any attack that targets civilians to send a political message is a terrorist attack, and we should condemn such attacks in no uncertain terms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, I have received feedback asking why the attacks by Hamas are considered terrorist attacks while the response by the IDF, which has resulted in civilian casualties, has not been called one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People are especially concerned about the IDF's response because of the mounting civilian deaths and casualties in Palestine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there is some debate in international legal circles about whether or not the law of armed conflict applies to Hamas' attacks since Hamas is not a state actor and Israel may be considered an occupying force in Gaza, I think the better view is that a state is entitled to take action against a non-state actor where that non-state actor poses a threat to the country or its people and there is no state that is able to contain or take action against that non-state actor.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was the legal basis for the US-led attack on Al Qaeda in Afghanistan after the 9-11 attacks, and I think as a small country, it is important for us to recognise this principle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Having said that, I would also state that the IDF is obliged to comply with international humanitarian law, which is also sometimes referred to as the law of war or the law of armed conflict, when responding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, while it is legitimate for the IDF to target Hamas' military assets and weapons, it is not legitimate to target civilians or object the civilian population needs for its daily survival.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, Hamas should also not be using civilians and civilian objects as human shields or co-locating military assets within them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, any attack must be proportional to the threat faced and the method used to respond should cause as little collateral damage as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Thus, where a precision strike is possible, that would spare civilian life and is able to achieve the military objective, that should be used over an option that would cause a large amount of collateral damage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, steps must be taken to minimise the impact of war on the civilian population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On this limb, there are conflicting views on Israel's direction to civilians to leave the war zone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One view is that this is Israel's attempt to comply with international law by asking civilians to leave the areas they intend to strike and because Hamas' military objectives are interspersed in the civilian population, this is a necessary step.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another view is that this is creating a wholesale and unnecessary displacement of the civilian population and could therefore be a breach of international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We should roundly condemn all breaches of international law by any participant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: No matter how emotionally upset we are, we should not abandon the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These laws are designed to curb our most savage instincts in the heat of battle.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This brings me to the next limb, which calls for all parties to ensure safety and security of civilians and to release all hostages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The points I had made in the earlier limbs apply here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This requires both actors to take steps to protect civilians from the effect of war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, there are allegations that the IDF has been conducting its war with disregard to the civilian population and the mounting death toll in Palestine is cited as evidence of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the other hand, Israel contends that Hamas is using the human population as a shield, including by placing part of its military tunnel system and command network under civilian objects.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Peter Beaumont from The Guardian, which is a newspaper that is generally sympathetic to the cause of Palestinian statehood, has said in an article on 30 October 2023, "Hamas' attitude towards civilians during the conflict in Gaza often appears to be cynical at best.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: After five conflicts with Israel since 2008, Hamas is well aware of the high potential for civilian deaths in fighting with Israeli forces – and has instrumentalised those fatalities in its messaging to the world." That is a damning statement from a newspaper that is otherwise supportive of the Palestinian cause.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I certainly hope that Hamas would take steps to prove these allegations are incorrect.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In order to do so, it must make sure it does not locate its military targets amongst the civilian population and does not take steps to prevent civilians leaving conflict areas if they wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are mainly civilians who have nothing to do with the conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Hamas is demanding the release of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli prisons in exchange for these civilians.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These prisoners have been convicted of a range of crimes, including terrorism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The observance of international law is particularly important for the weak and the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If Hamas and its combatants wish to hold the moral high ground in their fight for a Palestinian state, they must show that they respect international law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of us, myself included, are sympathetic to the cause of Palestinian statehood, but we respectfully say this is the wrong way to win the moral support for it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next limb, Sir, reiterates Singapore's long-standing commitment to a negotiated two-state solution consistent with the relevant United Nations (UN) Security Council Resolutions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the history of this land, now shared by the Palestinian and Jewish peoples, goes back thousands of years, I will focus on the more recent events that have brought these two peoples together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the end of World War I, the Ottoman Empire, which fought alongside Germany, was to be dismantled.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Palestine, which was under the rule of the Ottomans at this time, was transferred to the British, who administered it with a special mandate from the League of Nations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The area was therefore known as Mandatory Palestine from 1920 to the end of British rule in 1948.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Zionist cause, or movement for the creation of a Jewish nation, was also growing in Europe around this time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1917, the British has signed the Balfour declaration that promised its support for a Jewish "national home" in Palestine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Jewish people had been displaced from their homeland and had been dispersed in many parts of the world, including Europe, other parts of the Middle East and the US for centuries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Zionist movement grew from a longing by the Jewish community to return to their homeland and have a nation of their own.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: During the period of British rule, there were successive waves of Jewish immigration to Mandatory Palestine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the Jewish population grew and the demands for Jewish statehood got stronger, the local Palestinian population also started asserting themselves and there were various clashes between the Jewish and Palestinian communities during this period, with both demanding independent statehood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The UN first proposed a partition plan to divide the territory into two states, one Arab and one Jewish, in November 1947, with the British ready to relinquish control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, this agreement did not prevent conflict and civil war broke out shortly thereafter between the Jewish and Arab peoples in Palestine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The British terminated their mandate on 14 May 1948 and Israel declared independence on the same day.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next day, on 15 May 1948, the armies of five neighbouring Arab states invaded the area of Mandatory Palestine, starting the first Arab-Israeli war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the end of the war in 1949, which resulted in an armistice amongst the warring parties, Israel had more territory than the original UN partition plan while no independent state of Palestine emerged.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Instead, the remaining territory in the former Mandatory Palestine was held by Egypt and Jordan.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There followed large waves of immigration thereafter, both of Palestinian people out of Israeli territory as well as of Jewish people out of Arab territories and into the newly formed nation of Israel.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1967, Israel was once again attacked by its Arab neighbours and the resulting six-day war resulted in the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian lands of West Bank and the Gaza Strip, along with the Egyptian Sinai Peninsula and the Syrian Golan Heights.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are all territories which were part for the former Mandatory Palestine.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1973, there was yet another attack on Israel, the Yom Kippur War, from which Israel again emerged victorious.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although Israel's right to self-defence is universally acknowledged, its prolonged occupation of these territories was criticised, even by its own allies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most controversial aspect was the starting of Israeli settlements on the occupied territories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These settlements would make any subsequent disengagement of Israel from these lands more difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While relations between Israel and its Arab neighbours appeared moribund, signs of thawing emerged in the late 1970s, which culminated in the Camp David Summit brokered by US President Jimmy Carter in 1978.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Israel's Prime Minister Menachem Begin and Egyptian President Anwar Sadar met.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, at this time, many other Arab nations rejected this, as did the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next big step to Palestinian statehood came with the Oslo accords, which were signed in 1993 and 1995, this time involving Israeli Prime Minister Yithzak Rabin and PLO Leader Yaasar Arafat in a process facilitated by Norway.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both men won the Nobel Peace prize, along with Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres, for their efforts on Middle East peace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While this was a landmark move towards Palestinian statehood and peace in the Middle East, the leaders involved both faced criticisms from their own populations or, at least, from parts of them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Prime Minister Yithzak Rabin himself was tragically assassinated in November 1995 by Yigal Amir, a far-right extremist in Israel.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1996, elections were held in Palestine, with Yaasar Arafat emerging as President.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: His party, Fatah, won 55 of the 88 seats in parliament too.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 1999, the interim Palestinian Authority became permanent.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Israel, for its part, began its disengagement from the Gaza, with its settlers and military presence withdrawn by 2005.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Israel takes the position that it is no longer occupying the Gaza, although the UN and other agencies still views Israel as an occupying force because it maintains control over the Gaza's air and maritime space as well as several land borders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding this, the withdrawal of settlements and the military from the Gaza was a positive step for Palestinian statehood.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, the situation deteriorated following the 2006 parliamentary elections in Palestine, where Hamas won the majority of seats in the parliament, with most of their support coming from the Gaza.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The presidential elections had been won the year earlier, in 2005, by Mahmoud Abbas from the Fatah party.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Shortly after this, in 2007, after the failure of a national unity government involving Fatah and Hamas, fighting broke out between the two.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the course of this fighting, Hamas seized control of the Gaza with its militia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Palestinian Authority under President Mahmoud Abbas retained control of the West Bank.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Since then, the legal status of the Gaza has been grey.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is part of the Palestinian territory but under the de facto rule of Hamas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have been no presidential or parliamentary elections in Palestine since then, so neither Hamas nor Fatah can point to any recent mandate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The journey to Palestinian statehood is a complex one and in order to get there, it will be necessary both for Israel to play its part in withdrawing its military forces and settlements, as well as for the Palestinian peoples to show that they are capable of governing themselves and will not be a security threat to their neighbours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding this, it is my hope that both parties realise that the only long-term solution is one where there is a framework for both to co-exist securely.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I now come to the final limb of the Motion – urging all Singaporeans to safeguard and uphold our multiracial and multi-religious peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is a small country, far away from the conflict.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, when this conflict emerged, many in Singapore felt moved by it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I received many emails from residents, quite a number expressing sympathy for Hamas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Others I have spoken with said we should speak up more strongly for Israel's right of self-defence and should not be going soft on terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: People of different faiths live together, work together and even take steps to understand each other.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is not uncommon for people to visit places of worship even if they do not personally worship there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I myself have been to churches, mosques and temples, Hindu, Buddhist and Taoist, and I have always enjoyed learning about different religions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Let us come together, in solidarity, to support the cause for peace and security in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I hope for your support for this Motion.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: A copy of the said resolution has been distributed earlier for Members' reference.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In the time since the original Motion was tabled, the situation on the ground has been fluid, with more bloodshed and accusations surfacing even as we speak right now.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Members would be well aware of the complex historic background of the conflict.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Mr Vikram Nair has given a concise summary in his speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Members would also be well acquainted with the broad context of the current hostilities which I would not go into.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Some in this House would perhaps have also seen or watched the content that has emerged from the last four weeks with great alarm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As a parent, some of the images has left me stupefied and almost close to tears.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is not easy to watch and they were heart-rendering.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Whatever your support for either side in this conflict, you would have to be so cold and unfeeling to deem any of it acceptable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: To level such violence, barbarity, upon innocent civilians, especially children and the elderly, cannot be acceptable in any way or form.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: So, let us for a moment agree, that whatever our views on the conflict, that no civilian should be considered as a legitimate and deliberate target in any conflict.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I therefore call upon Members to express our deepest condolences to all innocent victims and civilians in this conflict – both Israeli and Palestinian – as well as other citizens that have been caught up in this conflagration.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We therefore need also to condemn those responsible for the terrorist acts and violations of international law.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The onslaught was to terrorise civilian targets and resulted in the deaths of over 1,400 Israelis and foreigners, mostly civilian.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Not since the Holocaust have so many Jewish lives been taken in a single day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: This includes 260 people killed at a music festival in Re'im, mostly young people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Throw your mind back to the Manchester Arena bombing of May 2017.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Over 240 people have also been taken hostage by Hamas.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: This is a war crime under Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, UN Resolution 34/146 International Convention against the Taking of Hostages and Article 8.2 of the ICC Statutes make it an offence as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Israel has pursued a legitimate right to defend itself against an organisation whose expressed intent is the annihilation of Israel.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: However, with that right provided by international law to defend itself comes the same obligations with the conduct of war.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Proportionality, a dirty word in Israel at the moment, has come to mind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is codified in the Geneva Conventions and is a core principle of international humanitarian law.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Proportionality states that while it is recognised that in operations against military objectives, civilian casualties are sometimes unavoidable, it is however imperative that the various warring parties – states and non-state armed groups alike – take all possible measures to minimise losses amongst the civilian population.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: If it is feared that an attack will cause excessive, disproportionate collateral damage to the concrete and direct military advantage expected, it should be cancelled or interrupted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We, must therefore considering these two circumstances: Firstly, demand the cessation of terror attacks and the immediate safe release of all hostages by Hamas; and Secondly, that Israel, in its pursuit of a legitimate defence, ensure full adherence to the norms of humanitarian law in the conduct of war, and avoiding a collective punishment of a population.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Thirdly, both sides are to ensure the safety and security as well as minimise the effect of conflict on all civilians and allow full access to humanitarian aid.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We have consistently advocated for the adherence to established international legal norms and principles, and we are not hesitant to speak forthrightly even to our own close allies when we believe they have transgressed these said principles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: When Russia invaded Ukraine, we stood in solidarity with Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We resolutely maintain that only through the collective respect for international law can rights and security of a small nation like ours be safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Over the years, Singapore has consistently voted in alignment with these principles and commitment to international law.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We have taken a firm stance on numerous resolutions related to Israel and Palestine.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: There are some who imply that Singapore is biased in our support of one party in this conflict.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Allow me to briefly recap the key occasions in which we have voted against a key ally in favour of peace and stability in the region in various UN General Assemblies over the past two decades.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The resolution called for an immediate and sustained humanitarian truce, provision of essential supplies to civilians in Gaza and for Israel to rescind its evacuation orders in the Gaza Strip.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The full text of the EoV is in the documents that were circulated earlier.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Moving back further, I would not go into the details, but this can be easily found in the UN Library 2017, 2011, 2004, 2003, 2002, 1997, even as far back as 1967 when the Israelis were extending support for our armed forces, we voted against the Israelis at the UN over matters of principles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: They possess the potential to reverberate and touch us here even in Singapore, while we observe the unfolding tragedy from what seems like a safe distance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: This reality underscores the profound impact that such conflicts can have on the fabric of our local community relations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It becomes imperative for us to recognise and address the potential toxicity that may seep into our own midst as a consequence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Perhaps, for many of us it is due to all too natural human instincts to be consumed by genuine concerns, influenced by our own religious affiliations, our relationships and our affinity as we digest the information flow in the news outlets and on the social media.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Yet we must be restrained in how we react.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We must appreciate that the social environment which we have built our society and our nation around that we must be vigilant against allowing these differences to fracture the unity of our diverse community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Members of the House, as representatives of our voters, it is therefore our duty to uphold these principles as well and ensure that our local relationships remain resilient, transcending the turbulence of global conflicts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We must unite at times like these, rather than seek to divide or seek political dividends.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In this vein, I have earlier in my PQs asked for the Home Affairs Ministry's assessment on the heightened risks to our social fabric and how we can better safeguard ourselves.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We must also engage in an open and honest conversation about the situation which is why Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Zhulkarnain and myself have decided to propose this Motion for debate today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Misguided beliefs and distorted narratives can further escalate tensions and lead to divisions within our community and, collectively, we must re-double our efforts to ensure that Singaporeans have access to reliable sources of information and are equipped to discern fact from fiction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: By doing so, we empower Singaporeans to make informed decisions and engage in constructive dialogues, even in the face of contentious global issues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Is it when we can see the sun?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: No, his answer was that darkness can only truly give way to light when we see the humanity in each other, when we can regard each other as a brother or a sister, despite our differences.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: While we do not have a simple quick-fix solution to it, we can play our part by not complicating it even further.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Here in Singapore, we need to make sure that we are always in the light of day – standing by our principles and regarding fellow Singaporeans regardless of our views as fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We must regard each other, of course, with respect, compassion and an acknowledgement of our kinship with each other as fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: May Singapore continue to stand as a shining example of tolerance and mutual understanding in our multicultural, multiracial and multi-religious community, a testament to the strength that emerges from our diversity.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: It is, therefore, important now, more than ever, that we uphold and protect this precious legacy, for it is the bedrock upon which our nation's peace and security is built.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of this Motion moved by my hon friend, Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like him and many others in this Chamber and across the world, I share the concerns about the plight of innocent civilians impacted.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What happened after that – the chaos and destruction in Gaza – is even more distressing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is a staggering 40% of the entire fatalities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are not even talking about children who have become orphans overnight, found themselves without a roof over their heads, or those who will have to live the rest of their lives permanently disabled.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are also about 30 Israeli children who have been taken hostage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These children must be returned to their parents and families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is now over a month and their safety is not just unknown but also uncertain, given the bombardment of Gaza.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Earlier last year, I welcomed the birth of my newborn son in difficult and emergency circumstances.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I saw firsthand in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (ICU), babies who are clinging on to their lives, fighting to survive every single day.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What I saw and read of the reports in Gaza, was the bombing of hospitals and health facilities, the cutting of electricity, medical aid and other necessities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The helpless children and newborn in the ICUs of such hospitals in Gaza would stand no chance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is compounded by the shutdown of Internet and communications essential to emergency services.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore could have just remained apathetic like the 45 other countries in the world who abstained in vote, but we stood up and put forward our position, voting on principles of humanity and international law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I thus support the amendments to this Motion proposed by Member Mr Alex Yam and co-sponsor of this Motion, which highlight this recent UN resolution.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is an issue, although complex and emotive, is very important to the peace and stability of not only the Middle East but the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not a religious or theological issue either; neither can we paint everyone with the same brush – not all Israelis voted for their government, not all Palestinians in Gaza are supporters of Hamas.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is also not an issue on Gaza alone but the rest of Palestine.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, in West Bank, where Hamas has no control, according to the humanitarian charity Save the Children, before 7 October, at least 38 Palestinian children have been killed this year, making it the deadliest year since records began.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This equates to more than one Palestinian child killed per week.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, at least six Israeli children were killed in the same period, three times more than last year.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is a long-standing issue with deep historical roots.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The world needs to do more globally to stop this cycle of violence and protect the children, whether they are Arabs or Jews, Israelis or Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2021, following the violence in Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa Mosque during Ramadan, I posed a question in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Minister Balakrishnan, in his responses, made it clear that Singapore's primary concern has always been the safety and security of civilians on all sides and that international law and agreements must be upheld.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, I asked about Singapore's efforts to support the Palestinian Authority.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This year during the Committee of Supply (COS) debates, I asked again on Singapore's role to alleviate the Palestinian-Israeli tensions, whether on our own or together with the Gulf countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where there were breaches of international law through illegal settlements and unilateral declarations of Jerusalem as capital city, Singapore has shown the courage of conviction to call it out through voting at the UN General Assembly resolutions ever since 1967.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's position has always been constant and principled.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a small country, we must always mean what we say and say what we mean.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can only take the side of principles and the law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But over the years, there are rules of engagement and international humanitarian law to ensure non-combatant casualties are kept to a minimal.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The law balances a nation's right to use deterrence as self-defence while mitigating the excessive brutalities and destruction that war would bring.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Assistant Professor Yuan Yi Zhu, of International Relations and International Law at Leiden University, the Netherlands, and a Research Fellow at Harris Manchester College, Oxford, recently stated: "International humanitarian law has broad acceptance because it seeks to mitigate the worst effects of armed conflict instead of banning it entirely.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If it's construed in a way that allows no practical military operations to take place, belligerents might just ignore it outright." International law, namely the Geneva Convention, is intended to protect innocent civilians during armed conflict and prohibits the targeting of civilians and essential objects indispensable to the survival of civilian population.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are four basic principles: first, distinction between non-combatants and others; second, military necessity; third, unnecessary suffering; and fourth, proportionality.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On necessity and proportionality, there is a grey line when collateral damages cross into collective punishment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: International humanitarian law ensures that collective punishment for a crime committed by an individual is forbidden.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For the current conflict, in the face of what has been reported or what appears to be breaches of humanitarian law, I am deeply distressed and concerned because I am only human.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I remain calm because I believe in justice and the due process of the law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After the dust settles, a fuller investigation of the evidence and such breaches of international law can and must be made.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this age of technological advancement and social media, evidence can be found, witnesses can corroborate and false information can be sifted out so that any breaches of international law would one day come to light and the perpetrators would be brought to the International Courts of Justice for their day of reckoning.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Against this backdrop, we must continue to have faith and continue to abide by our principles and the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Palestinian civilians in Gaza are now facing a health crisis sparked by the destruction of public infrastructure, such as hospitals, ambulances and medical supplies that were blocked.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The UN on 2 November stated that "Gaza is running out of time" and it is a critical time for Palestinians right now.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Innocent children have become victims of the relentless violence of war.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those caught in the middle of the conflict are Palestinians from different religions and backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Palestinian civilians who have done no wrong are yearning for peace and prosperity for their families and children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But now, they are facing a bleak future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need compassion and protection of the Palestinian civilians' rights.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over the years, I have raised this issue in Parliament about humanitarian efforts and Singapore's support towards the peace process in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was thankful when a humanitarian channel was recently opened for supplies to enter Gaza even if it was for a brief period.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am also touched by the encouraging amount of donation for humanitarian aid in Gaza, not only from our Malay/Muslim community, but from all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This demonstrates our collective effort regardless of race, religion or age.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Spiritually, our Malay/Muslim community has also prayed for peace in our mosques through special prayer sessions and reciting the supplication Qunut Nazilah during prayer.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, Pergas organized the first special prayer session at the Kassim Mosque.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also attended the special prayers at Al-Firdaus mosque with our foreign workers and at the Al-Khair mosque with Chua Chu Kang residents.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many of our old and young congregants were also there.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope Singapore will support the proposal to bring anyone who is guilty and who violates international law, so that they will face justice and a day of reckoning in future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I spoke in Malay about the efforts of the community to support the humanitarian cause in Gaza, together with our nation.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our Mufti exemplified leadership in extending not only compassion and our condolences for those who have lost lives and loved ones but also our collective condemnation against violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During this period, our religious leaders have also guided our asatizah and community in handling the deluge of information and emotional impact on all of us through the khutbah sermons during Friday prayers and religious guidance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mufti's leadership showcases to the world that Islam emphasises peace and compassion for all.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there is a view questioning the need for such religious guidance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard what is the Government's position on such views, especially in conflicts which are complex and go beyond the religious realm?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We cannot be pulled into a partisan fight pitting one against the other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us have the conviction of courage to do the right thing and show empathy for all affected.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us not allow conflicts overseas to sow discords of disharmony amongst us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us remain united with fellow Singaporeans to stand side by the side – on the side of humanity and compassion.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Quoting from Martin Luther King, "Returning hate for hate multiplies hate, adding deeper darkness to a night already devoid of stars.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that." Mr Speaker, Sir, I support this Motion and beg to move.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote, "The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is the biggest problem plaguing the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a running sore that oozes pus all the time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To end the conflict, there has to be a two-state solution – one for the Israelis and one for the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Palestinian state must also be economically and politically viable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its people must feel that they have a reasonable chance of making a success out of their country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only then will they have a vested interest in keeping peace in this troubled region." "Because of the pro-Israel policy the Jewish lobby has succeeded in forging for America, a hardline stance is allowed to prevail in the Israeli leadership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This can have adverse and irreversible effects on the peace process.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By building settlements in the occupied territories, for example, Israel is slowly but surely annexing land that would be handed over to the Palestinians in any potential deal between the two sides." "Ultra-conservatives in Israel believe the settlements bring Israel closely to its rightful historical borders as laid out in the Hebrew bible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They believe recovering the land is ordained by God, no less.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The settlements represent an unwelcomed revision to an already complicated status quo.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are causing the prospects of any future possible deal to become ever remote." Mr Lee continues, "With every passing day, a permanent solution to the conflict becomes less likely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The United Nations has declared the Israeli settlements a violation of international law, describing them as a creeping annexation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Without the Americans putting pressure on Israel, there is no end in sight for the conflict." Mr Lee also warns, "The conflict also serves as an evergreen cause which Jihadists can exploit as part of their propaganda efforts to attract young recruits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The sight of dead children being pulled from the rubble, their parents weeping, is something no sane human being could ever wish for anyone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why should we in Singapore even be speaking in Parliament about what is happening in Israel and the occupied territories, including Gaza?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A conflict more than 8,000 kilometers away has prompted Singaporeans from all communities to speak out and donate money to assist those in Gaza who are in dire circumstances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is clear that Singaporeans care and are very concerned about what is happening there.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will make three points in my speech, taking reference from the Workers' Party (WP)'s statement on the conflict on 18 October 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will repeat the statement for the record without reference to the footnotes in the statement. "The Workers' Party Members of Parliament have received many emails and representations from Singaporeans calling for an immediate end to hostilities and the delivery of humanitarian aid into the Gaza Strip." "Previous military action in the Gaza Strip undertaken by the Israel Defence Forces in response to militant operations including by Hamas have been marked by overwhelming disproportionality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We fear this reality will repeat itself in the coming days, weeks and months." "The flagrant disregard of the Geneva Convention, the United Nations Charter and other international legal instruments; including the occupation of land taken in war by any sovereign nation – is not in Singapore's national interests." "The killing of non-combatants, women and children by any country or organisation, in the name of war, deserves no less than absolute condemnation." "The Workers' Party supports Singapore's long-held position that a two-state solution consistent with UN Security Council (UNSC) resolutions is the only viable path to a durable, just and comprehensive resolution to the long-standing conflict between Israel and Palestine." "In particular, UNSC Resolution 242 which is supported by Singapore, calls for the withdrawal of Israel from Palestinian territories occupied since the 1967 war, in exchange for a lasting peace with its neighbours." "Worryingly, the continuing conflict in Israel and Palestine is likely to increase attacks against Jews and Muslims elsewhere, raising the prospect of radicalisation far beyond the Middle East, making the world more unsafe and dangerous for all countries, particularly where multiracial and multicultural communities live in peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All Singaporeans should be aware and mindful of this possibility and play an active part to prevent it from happening on our shores." "We call on Israel to reject the collective punishment of innocent civilians, cease all military operations in the Gaza Strip and to allow for the transit of humanitarian aid into Gaza forthwith.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: De-escalation by all parties must be followed by a withdrawal of Israel from the occupied territories, followed by serious negotiations to achieve a lasting peace in the Holy Land – a peace that legitimises the existence of the state of Israel and establishes a viable Palestinian state." By the time the WP released its statement on 18 October, ordinary Singaporeans were troubled and even agitated about the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many wrote to the WP Members of Parliament and continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the assessment of the WP, one reason that precipitated this frustration was the perception of a dominant narrative at that point in the West and other advanced economies to focus only on the actions of Hamas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There can be no reason to target, kill or take civilians hostage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it is important to point out that the West's one-dimensional narrative was inadequate and incomplete because it suggested that the Israel-Palestine conflict started on 7 October 2023, with the killing of innocent civilians in Israel.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Absent was context – context of Israel's occupation and subjugation of the occupied territories, a matter that has not been resolved for decades, nor was there any reflection on past UN fact-finding missions to Gaza in the aftermath of previous Israel-Hamas conflicts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nor was there any consideration of the impact of the wanton expansion of settlements in the occupied territories by successive right-wing Israeli governments, which de-legitimised the right of a Palestinian people, making any future peace even harder to reach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, these omissions, amongst others, operated to decontextualise the tragedy that befell Israel and their people on 7 October 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I assume Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Zhulkarnain will agree with me that the Israel-Hamas conflict is a subset of a larger struggle that arises out of the absence of a political resolution to the conflict between Israel and the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I invite all three Members to disagree with me now and for the record, if they do not agree with this statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first objective of the WP's statement of 18 October was to put out this seemingly obvious fact – that the latest eruption in hostilities between Israel and the Palestinians should not be seen in isolation even as we condemn the killing of civilians by any country or organisation, including Hamas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Having done so, it was important to state that this latest outbreak of hostilities between Israel and Hamas was not new.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Since the withdrawal of Israeli settlements from the Gaza Strip in 2006, four other major conflicts have broken out between Israel and Hamas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The tragedy that is befalling the people of Gaza today is a continuation of what has happened many times before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the end, the story on the Palestinian side is always far more gruesome in scale – overwhelming casualties, with a large number of children among the dead.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only the ill-informed could have thought that the latest instalment was going to be any different.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As one senior former Israeli Defence Forces commander told me once, the Israeli way of war in the Gaza Strip is to strike hard so that the Palestinians learn a lesson they never forget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, they live in fear and, as a result, are deterred from ever attacking Israel again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With such an approach to warfare, one that invokes collective punishment in the name of self-defence, the death of many innocent Palestinians is all but certain.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Far from deterring future attacks on the Israeli state, this disproportionate response gives birth to a new generation of Palestinians that seek to avenge their forebears and some of whom see martyrdom as something to aspire to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A second important aspect of the WP statement was to identify the threat of the latest edition of the Israel-Hamas conflict to multiracial and multicultural societies and communities like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of radicalisation and the prospect of uncalled for and senseless attacks against Jews and Muslims all over the world and a more unsafe world as a result, cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans should be alive to this and not fall prey to calls, especially online, that target Jews or Muslims.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the call for a negotiated two-state solution to the conflict, consistent with UN Resolutions, is a clear way forward, we all know that the reality is more complex and layered, and getting to this outcome will be a struggle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, many months ago, the most famous historian of his generation, Yuval Harari, a Jew living in Israel, was quoted as saying on the BBC that "my house is burning".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to Hamas' unprovoked attack, an intense political battle had been taking place for Israel's soul.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Deep political fissures over a fundamental tenet of democracy, the separation of powers, pitted many elements of Israeli society against the plans of a right-wing government led by Benjamin Netanyahu.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote Yuval Harari from a piece he penned for The Financial Times in July this year, "To understand events in Israel, there is just one question to ask: what limits the power of government?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Robust democracies rely on a whole system of checks and balances, but Israel lacks a constitution, an Upper House in the Parliament, a federal structure, or any other check on government power except one, the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Netanyahu government plans to pass the first in a series of laws that will neutralise the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it succeeds, it will gain unlimited power." The International Institute for Strategic Studies, which hosts the annual Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, reported that between March and July this year, Israeli air force reservists refused to keep up their training hours, helicopter instructor pilots refused to report for duty, and active reservists in the Special Forces refused to volunteer for service, all in the protest of the country's direction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These differences in Israeli society should remind those of us far removed that not all Israelis think alike, and that there are Jews and Israelis who may not necessarily agree with the right-wing political leadership on issues that include pursuing a strategy of settlement expansion that seeks to unilaterally change facts on the ground.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be incorrect to think that all Jews and Israelis are monolithic in their views, even as their desire for a homeland where they can live in peace without being subjected to terrorist attacks is shared by all Israelis and friends of Israel, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The nuances are no different in the case of Palestinian organisations that operate in the Gaza Strip and in the other occupied territories.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This point was shrewdly emphasised by the Palestine ambassador to Malaysia last month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, he thanked Malaysians for their steadfast support for the Palestinian cause but, on the other, warned them to channel their donations and support carefully, lest they reach the wrong hands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some months ago, in a different context, he was on record noting that there were sectarian issues, such as internal politics involving the Palestinian population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For those who are familiar with this, the Palestinian National Authority and Hamas, for example, have different approaches to achieve their goals, even if Israel has deemed the Palestinian Authority as supporting Hamas after the latter's actions on 7 October 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Israel-Hamas confrontation and broader conflict look set to continue for some time, Singaporeans should be aware that in view of our multiracial and multi-religious society, this conflict will test us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But it should not be allowed to compromise our multiracial and multi-religious peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Singaporeans, we should not analyse a political issue through religious lenses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For us, it is a humanitarian issue, and both Israel and the Palestinians deserve to live in peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our contribution is a humanitarian one, to advocate and support calls to stop the killing, particularly of civilians and children, and to support the international community in reaching a lasting settlement between Israel and the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my third and final point on the importance of international law for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both the parties directly involved in the conflict, as well as the rest of the international community, must know Singapore's position and our firm belief in international law and our desire for the protection of human life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We endorse the UN Charter and other international agreements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We support them because our survival depends on them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, Singapore has made its position on the Russia-Ukraine conflict clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We took particular umbrage at the Russian claim that its aggression in Ukraine was justified because of historical errors and crazy decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The principles and reasons for doing so are readily apparent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If some religious group, militant organisation or other country justified its aggression on something other than international law, we would have to aggressively stand against such perspectives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, some group or organisation in a neighbouring country may argue that Singapore has been part of the Malay archipelago for centuries and, therefore, should expect to be occupied and annexed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: International law is clear that this cannot be so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A price that has proven and will continue to prove to be a high one for the world well beyond the borders of Israel and Palestine.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: "I am not truly free if I am taking away someone else's freedom.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as surely as I am not free when my freedom is taken from me.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For to be free is not merely to cast off one's chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others" – Nelson Mandela.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a fight in distant lands, but here, in Singapore, many feel empathy and distress as the news, photos and videos fill our social media feeds and our daily consciousness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you are truly engaged with the breadth of society, you will see a range of views and levels of awareness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A number of our youths, in particular, have written to me.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They seek an outlet to use their voices to do something, anything, for they cannot unsee the suffering in Gaza, they cannot reconcile it with our life as per normal and our precious peace here, and we cannot sit silent.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is reported that almost half of the Gazan population is aged 18 and under, and we feel for the mothers who have lost their children, for the men who have buried their brothers in mass graves, for the elderly who are too frail to move, and for the children whose normalcy is rubble and dust.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These divides arose many years, even before 7 October 2023, and have no easy answers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One might point to a time in history and someone else would go back a few years for a different view.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, there are religious bearings, but there are Christians, Jews and Muslims on both sides of the border.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot ignore the political, historical, land and security dimensions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a lot to unpack, but a few things are clear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, the growing humanitarian crisis in Gaza needs to be addressed urgently.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Refugee camps, hospital areas and schools have not been spared from airstrikes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The UN relief agency, UNRWA and Committee to Protect Journalists shared that eight workers and media personnel have been killed.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, even in a fight, there are rules.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: International humanitarian law, as set out in the Geneva Conventions and similar treaties, has been forged from the bitter ashes of world wars as a practical balance between the security and military requirements of a state, and the protection of humans.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, Sir, we agree that any and all violence and kidnapping of innocent civilians are wrong.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But while a state has a right to self-defence, this must be tempered by proportionality.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parties must distinguish between combatants and civilians, and many have asked: is the loss of so many innocent non-military personnel proportionate?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When will the collective punishment against the Palestinian people end?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, both sides must work towards a durable peace with the support of the international community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not the first time that violence has broken out.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The result of these prolonged cycles is a gradually reduced confidence and support for a long-lasting two-state solution, according to public polls among both Israeli and Palestinian people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can people in positions of power in Gaza and Israel come to the table to negotiate for peace with open hearts?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The international community must direct resources to invest in peace, so as to manage tensions at all stages of the conflict curve, involve independent parties with the conviction to see this through, prioritising local communities before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is not the first time that violence has broken out and the result of these prolonged cycles is a gradually reduced confidence and support for a long-lasting two-state solution, according to public polls among both Israeli and Palestinian people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can people in positions of power in Gaza and Israel come to the table to negotiate for peace with open hearts?" The international community must direct resources to invest in peace so as to manage tensions at all stage of the conflict curve – involve independent parties with the conviction to see this through, priorisiting local communities, before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   The crisis in Gaza is deteriorating due to rising tensions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many people around the world, including those in Singapore, have come forward to appeal for the violence to stop immediately.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, humanitarian aid alone is not enough to repair and rebuild a community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To achieve lasting peace for all parties, a long-term solution should be worked out.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, we are also aware that harmony is something that is difficult to achieve and very fragile, as it requires sacrifices and an understanding that is built over decades.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a small nation, we must uphold integrity and be pragmatic because this will determine our future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To quote the UN Chief's speech, we are aware that the Hamas attack did not happen in isolation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although many have mentioned the October 7 incident, we will still remember the sufferings of the people of Gaza from October 6 and the days before that.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although we acknowledge that the Hamas attack on October 7 in Israel is wrong, we mourn the loss of lives in Gaza and the West Bank and feel the injustice.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Singaporeans including our youths have asked about the Singapore Government's views on the killing of civilians in Gaza, as well as other immediate actions, that the Government can take to try and stop the violence before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our stand is consistent with the principles that are necessary for Singapore survival.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In navigating tensions, we do not unequivocally support one side over another.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We advocate for an inclusive, rules-based, multilateral order as a system to have recourse to when necessary.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But, Sir, even as we have voted in support of resolution over the years including for statehood and against illegal settlements, it appears that little progress has been made.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We find ourselves in deepening divides with worsening intensities of the violence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What more can be done to enforce the rules which give us order?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government does not act alone in promoting peace and providing humanitarian aid.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A team of four has followed the aid to Egypt donating it to the Palestine Red Crescent.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is our Singaporean way; not just speaking about harmony during times of peace, but being brave through our differences and rallying together during times of crisis around our common humanity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Here, in Singapore, which has been ranked as one of the most religiously diverse countries in the world, we know this intimately.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We each desire the freedom to express our different identities, but this means in turn that we are committed to seeing that others with different beliefs can express their identities authentically as well.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As an advisor to the recently concluded Harmony Circles Refresh work group together with Minister of State Alvin Tan, I know that harmony does not occur by chance.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We work for it every day as a people, through compromise and acceptance and by learning from each other what makes our beliefs so secret?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We treasure the safety of living in peace with others whose beliefs are different from ours while being united as one Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This peace is made possible in no small part due to the selfless commitment to inter-faith harmony from our religious leaders across different faiths.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mutual respect and the willingness of these leaders to stand in solidarity create a quiet but steadfast example.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notably, in the Inter-Religious Organisation of Singapore, 10 faiths, such as Buddhism, Islam, Christianity and Judaism, regularly come together and exchange views.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a world where rhetoric and sound bites go viral on social media and longer messages run the risk of getting twisted, where popularity is currency and common ground is the first casualty in a fight, it takes courage to stand for peace and conviction to nurture it, even when the position may be hard to swallow.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I am grateful for the discernment and compassion of our faith leaders in society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The exchange of letters between faith leaders and Singapore during times like these demonstrate commitment to protect the precious collective peace that we share.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even as emotions run high, let us not give in to Islamophobia, anti-Semitism or other forms of discrimination in our places of worship, our schools, our workplaces and society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Peace breaks down when anger consumes and we feel that we cannot communicate.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important for us Singaporeans to grow in our ability to seek understanding, step up quickly and communicate in managing a crisis while always having our nation's interests at our core.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, how can we encourage safe outlets for the expression, processing and validation of emotions and the promotion of understanding even when we disagree?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can our leaders at all levels in our communities and places of worship be better equipped to guide on such matters, which have implications on our shores?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the front lines of conflict are increasingly digital, how do we care for, equip and soothe a society where many spend approximately seven hours a day online.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this fractious world, Singapore is a small voice.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is easy to believe that we do not have a stake or that we cannot do much.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our sovereignty and safety are tied to a fair rules-based world order and a common humanity.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the past few weeks, we have seen the good in humanity as well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the ensuing retaliation by Israel in the Gaza Strip over the past month demands critical scrutiny and a response from the International Community including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More than 1.5 million people have been internally displaced and Northern Gaza has been laid siege by Israel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Israel said it dropped 6,000 bombs on the Gaza Strip in just the first week of the war.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This number is surely much higher now topping the record number of bombs the US dropped in Afghanistan in the whole of 2019.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The WP supports Israel's right to defend itself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this right must be wielded within the bounds of international humanitarian law, ensuring that the sanctity of human life particularly that of civilians and children is upheld even in the midst of a war.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Israel was successful in securing its border with Gaza within days of the assault but it continues to destroy civilian infrastructure, displace hundreds of thousands of people and cut off supplies of water and electricity in the Gaza Strip.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Israel must recognise that executing this asymmetric response will only breed further hatred of it among the Palestinian population and provide fuel for extremists both in Gaza and around the world, perpetrating the cycle of violence and suffering.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Former US President Barack Obama said that upholding international law and avoiding to every extent possible the death or suffering of civilian populations is, "vital for building alliances and shaping international opinion, all of which are critical for Israel's long-term security." Israel therefore, must adhere strictly to the laws of war not only for the sake of the suffering Palestinians but also for its own security.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Proportionality, distinction and necessity must guide its military actions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Hamas must also immediately and unconditionally release all Israeli and foreign hostages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Failure to do so will only prolong this war and lead to a greater loss of life and hardening of hearts on both sides.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore may be a small country, but we must do everything within our capacity working alongside countries in the region and international agencies to deliver essential humanitarian aid to the suffering people of Gaza during this current conflict.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our assistance must go beyond alleviating immediate suffering for the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We can also contribute to post-conflict reconstruction and development by offering more technical assistance to the Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, in education, public housing, urban planning, water management and tackling corruption.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Under the auspices of the Singapore Cooperation Programme, Singapore has provided training for many Palestinian officials.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must follow through with this pledge, as this technical assistance will be needed more than ever during the reconstruction following the war.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our long-standing ties with Israel go back to our early days of Independence and National Service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore also has good relations with the Palestinians and with influential Muslim-majority countries such as Egypt, Jordan, Türkyie, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Bahrain, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, some of which have established diplomatic relations with Israel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our longstanding ties with Israel go back to our early days of Independence and National Service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore also has good relations with the Palestinians and with influential Muslim-majority countries, such as Egypt, Jordan, Turkey, the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, some of which have established diplomatic relations with Israel.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore was also the first country to sign a free trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's diplomatic standing and trade relations with these nations place us in a position to play a constructive role towards pushing for a long-term solution for peace in the region.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should work with like-minded partners to help establish the foundations for enduring peace between the Israelis and Palestinians and advocate for the implementation of the two-state solution.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We should seek opportunities to facilitate greater dialogue among all stakeholders, including hosting high-level summits between Israeli and Palestinian leaders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore could provide a neutral venue for peace talks, away from the conflict zone.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This potential peacemaking role is consistent with past initiatives.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, Singapore was the backdrop for the first-ever summit between the leaders of the US and North Korea.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Before that, in 2015, we facilitated the landmark meeting between the presidents of China and Taiwan.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, our thinktanks, like the Middle East Institute, could play host to more Track 2 economic exchanges and business forums between the Israelis and Palestinians.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These less formal dialogues are essential in building understanding and sharing Singapore's experiences in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Your passion, concern and call for a more balanced, humane approach have been instrumental in shaping our collective voice on this matter.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us unite in supporting efforts that foster peace, dialogue and understanding.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
